query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single intervention of cryogenic rolling followed by a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment will refine the coarse lamellar colonies of a eutectic high-entropy alloy into a hierarchical microstructure with ultrafine grains, leading to enhanced crack arresting at internal boundaries and thus simultaneously boosting both yield strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies with continuous internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply cryogenic rolling (i.e., deformation at cryogenic temperatures to induce high strain and stored energy) followed by a tailored annealing process that promotes partial recrystallization and grain refinement while preserving the lamellar architecture.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing conditions; processing under a significant (>80-90%) thickness reduction via cryo-rolling, followed by annealing at a temperature low enough to prevent complete recrystallization (conditions similar to those reported in related work, e.g., PMC5818523).
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, dual-phase hierarchical lamellar microstructure featuring ultrafine grains within each lamella and a higher density of grain and phase boundaries that act as barriers to microcrack propagation.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling increases the stored strain energy and promotes deformation-induced defects, and the subsequent controlled annealing leads to a refined microstructure without full grain growth. The increased density of interfaces retards crack propagation, while the refined grain size provides enhanced work hardening, thereby synergistically improving strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the conventional processing baseline, the alloy processed with the cryogenic rolling and annealing regimen will exhibit a statistically significant increase in both yield/tensile strength and tensile elongation at room temperature.
generation.baseline: EHEA samples produced via traditional warm-rolling and annealing that show high strength but limited ductility due to the propensity for microcrack initiation at coarse, continuous lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect depends on preserving the dual-phase lamellar structure; annealing temperatures that are too high (leading to complete recrystallization or lamella coarsening) might abolish the microstructural benefits. Additionally, the approach is effective only if the alloy’s chemistry supports the formation of a duplex lamellar structure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing parameters (degree of deformation, precise annealing temperature and duration) needed to optimize the microstructure and the quantitative improvements in strength and ductility remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy: one processed using conventional warm-rolling and annealing (baseline) and the other processed via cryogenic rolling followed by controlled annealing. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural analyses (using SEM/TEM) on both sets to compare grain size, phase distribution, and internal boundary characteristics.
measurements: Crack initiation and propagation patterns during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed samples do not show both a statistically significant increase in strength and ductility relative to the baseline samples, or if microstructural characterization does not reveal a refined hierarchical lamellar structure with increased crack-arresting interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing

Abstract: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
